rationale: The entry's core — islands as peoples set apart out of the sea of nations — rests on a well-evidenced premise (sea = peoples, glossed explicitly in Rev 17:15 and confirmed by parallelism in Isa 17:12, Ps 65:7, Luke 21:25, Hag 2:6-7) and carries every printed citation: Gen 10:5's isles are peoples 'divided... every one after his tongue' (distinct peoples, not raw mass); Isa 42:4 and 51:5 state the 'waiting for God's law' clause verbatim; Isa 11:11 has the remnant preserved in and recovered from the islands; Job 22:30 (KJV, the translation supplied) says outright that 'the island of the innocent' is 'delivered by the pureness of thine hands,' directly supporting the preservation clause; and Rev 16:20 draws a genuine verbal asymmetry — islands 'fled away' while mountains 'were not found' — which coheres with the entry's differential fates given mountains = kingdoms. The strongest counter (distant Gentile coastlands as a metonym for the ends of the earth, with Rev 16:20 as generic cosmic upheaval) shares the core referent for the Isaiah and Genesis texts — distinct peoples among humanity who wait for God's law — so it does not contradict the core; it differs mainly in grounding the figure in geographic remoteness rather than symbolic separation. It also has no explanation for Job 22:30 ('island of the innocent' delivered is unintelligible on a geographic reading) and must split the word's meaning by context, whereas the book explains all six printed citations under one identification. No supplied text is inexplicable under the book's core, so the entry stands as the best explanation of the printed evidence.
book_core_identification: An island/isle symbolizes a set-apart (separated, holy) people standing up out of the sea of peoples — covenant ground rising above the mass of the nations, i.e., peoples distinguished from ungoverned humanity and turned toward God.
book_secondary_elaborations: The isles 'wait for God's law' — the set-apart peoples are oriented toward and expectant of God's instruction (Isa 42:4; 51:5).

The isles are 'preserved while surrounding kingdoms fall' — at the final shaking the islands are removed to safety ('fled away') while the mountains/kingdoms are destroyed ('not found'), supported by Rev 16:20, Job 22:30's deliverance of 'the island of the innocent,' and Isa 11:11's remnant recovered from the islands.
The isles rise 'from the sea of nations' — the identification presupposes the sea = peoples/nations symbol (Rev 17:15).
chapter_only_objections: Rev 6:14 applies the identical predicate ('moved out of their places') to both mountains and islands, which strains the chapter's differential-fates argument: if 'moved' means carried out of harm for islands, consistency would demand the same for mountains, which the chapter reads as destroyed kingdoms.

The chapter's claim that the Hebrew 'iy usage 'never bends' overreaches: passages such as Ezek 26-27 (Tyre a 'merchant of the people for many isles') and 'isles afar off' (Jer 31:10; Isa 66:19) foreground commerce and geographic distance rather than covenant set-apartness.

The Job 22:30 unpointed-consonants argument depends on the KJV rendering; most modern translations read the particle as a negative ('him that is not innocent'), so the chapter's lexical inference is contestable outside the KJV.
The statistical claim that roughly three of four 'sea' verses carry or deepen the symbol is asserted, not demonstrated, and cannot be verified from the excerpts.
strongest_counter_interpretation: 'Iyyim/isles denotes distant coastlands and their peoples — a stock metonym for the remote Gentile nations and the farthest reaches of the earth who will hear of and receive God's salvation (Isa 41:1; 42:4; 49:1; 51:5; Gen 10:5) — while in Revelation 16:20 the islands, paired with mountains, are cosmic/geopolitical features removed in universal judgment, not a preserved people; occurrences are read geographically or contextually rather than under one fixed symbol.
counter_core_identification: Islands = distant Gentile nations/coastlands, standing for the worldwide reach of God's purposes; in apocalyptic contexts, features of the world order removed in judgment.
material_core_denial: To defeat the entry the counter would need to deny that the isles are peoples distinguished from the mass of nations and oriented toward God's law, and to show that Rev 16:20's islands share the mountains' destruction rather than being delivered. On the first point the counter does not actually deny the referent — its 'distant Gentile nations' are themselves distinct peoples awaiting God's law (Isa 42:4; 51:5) — and on the second it must ignore the verse's own verbal asymmetry and cannot account for Job 22:30's delivered 'island of the innocent' or Isa 11:11's remnant preserved in the islands.
counter_case: The Hebrew 'iyyim lexically means coastlands, and the recurring qualifier 'afar off' (Jer 31:10; Isa 66:19) shows distance, not holiness, is the operative connotation.
Gen 10:5 calls them 'isles of the Gentiles' — Japhethite maritime nations, not covenant peoples.
Isa 11:11 lists the islands alongside Assyria, Egypt, Pathros, Cush, Elam, Shinar, and Hamath — a geographic catalogue of remote regions, fitting a locative rather than symbolic sense.

Rev 16:20 pairs islands with mountains in a cosmic-upheaval formula (cf. Rev 6:14, where both are 'moved out of their places' together), so both are most naturally removed in judgment rather than given opposite fates.
Job 22:30 is widely regarded by modern translators as containing a negative particle ('he delivers even him that is not innocent'), removing 'island' from the verse entirely.
book_explanatory_advantages: One consistent identification explains all six printed citations, matching the book's demonstrated method of uniform symbol definitions (as with sea = peoples, explicitly glossed in Rev 17:15).

Job 22:30 as supplied (KJV) — 'He shall deliver the island of the innocent' — is directly explained by the entry (a set-apart innocent one delivered) and is inexplicable on the geographic/distant-nations reading.
Isa 11:11 supports the preservation clause: the remnant is kept in and recovered from the islands of the sea.
Rev 16:20's verbal asymmetry (islands 'fled away' vs. mountains 'not found') is predicted by the entry's differential fates, given the adjudicated mountain = kingdom symbol in the same system.
Gen 10:5's division 'every one after his tongue, after their families, in their nations' fits 'peoples marked off from one another,' the separation mechanic the entry asserts.

The entry preserves rather than contradicts the common Isaian datum — the isles wait for God's law (Isa 42:4; 51:5) — while supplying a mechanic (land standing out of the sea of peoples) that the 'remote nations' metonym leaves unexplained.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Matches the lexical sense of 'iyyim as coastlands and the 'afar off' distance idiom found elsewhere in the prophets.
Reads Rev 16:20 in step with Rev 6:14's pairing of mountains and islands, avoiding the differential-fates strain.
Aligns with the majority of translations and commentaries, requiring no revision of Job 22:30's disputed rendering.
decisive_sources: Revelation 17:15 (chapter evidence: waters = peoples, multitudes, nations, tongues — the premise for reading islands as what stands out of that sea)
Isaiah 42:4 — 'the isles shall wait for his law' (verbatim support for the entry's waiting clause)
Isaiah 51:5 — 'the isles shall wait upon me, and on mine arm shall they trust'
Genesis 10:5 — isles as peoples divided by tongue, family, nation
Job 22:30 (KJV) — 'He shall deliver the island of the innocent' (preservation clause; unexplainable on the geographic counter)
Isaiah 11:11 — remnant recovered from the islands of the sea (preservation of the set-apart)
Revelation 16:20 — islands 'fled away' vs. mountains 'not found' (verbal asymmetry supporting differential fates)
unresolved_objections: The differential reading of Rev 16:20 remains contestable: mainstream exegesis treats 'fled away' and 'not found' as synonymous removal (cf. Rev 20:11, not supplied, where 'fled away' and 'no place found' describe the same event), and Rev 6:14 applies one predicate to both features.
The entry's 'set-apart' gloss underplays the distance connotation ('isles afar off') that is prominent in the prophets and central to the common interpretation.
Job 22:30's support depends on the KJV rendering; the modern-critical reading of the particle would remove that witness.
